messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
Minh was thirty-two when his life was interrupted by a diagnosis of myocarditis—a sudden, severe inflammation of the heart muscle that landed him in the cardiac intensive care unit for two weeks. He had been healthy, active, a UX designer who prided himself on the fine-grained logic of his wireframes. But during a routine morning run he felt a crushing pressure in his chest, and by the time the paramedics arrived he was convinced he was dying. The hospital became a blur of beeping monitors, cold stethoscopes, and doctors whose faces he could not read. He remembers the moment a cardiologist said “we need to talk about what we found” and the long pause before the next sentence—a silence he has replayed hundreds of times.

He survived. His heart recovered. But something in him did not.

Now, three years later, Minh lives inside a kind of coiled vigilance he cannot shake. His body feels perpetually on alert, as if the ground beneath him might give way at any second. When he sits at his desk prototyping a new app interface, his shoulders are hunched, his jaw tight; he catches himself holding his breath. The sensation has become so familiar that he barely notices it, except when his wife touches his arm and he flinches. She tells him he is safe, that the doctors cleared him, that the inflammation is gone. Minh hears the words, but they land somewhere outside him, on a surface that cannot absorb them. He has come to believe that safety is something other people get to feel; for him, there is only the before and the after, and the after feels permanently contaminated.

He avoids hospitals with the same instinctive force he once used to avoid a buggy code release. His work commute routes him around the medical district, even if it adds twenty minutes. When his wife suggested a routine physical, Minh felt a spike of hot fear that surprised him with its intensity. He refused. Physical examinations, blood draws, the smell of antiseptic—any of it could pull him back into that room with the cardiologist and the long pause. He has also stopped running. He stopped any activity that raises his heart rate, because the flutter in his chest, once so benign, now feels like a warning. He avoids thinking about the illness directly, but the thoughts arrive anyway, unbidden: he will be sitting in a meeting and the memory of the ambulance siren cuts through, or he will see a headline about sudden cardiac death and his focus dissolves for the rest of the day.

The worst moments come when something takes longer than expected. A delayed train, a colleague who is late to a stand-up, a software build that hangs on a loading screen—each one triggers a cascade of certainty: something bad is happening. Minh knows, rationally, that a loading screen is just a loading screen. But his body does not. His pulse quickens, his breathing becomes shallow, and the thought comes: *this is the moment the news shifts, the moment everything falls apart again.* He cannot trust the ordinary passage of time; it has become a trap.

He has begun to feel hollow. Not sad, exactly, but emptied. He told his therapist last week that he feels dead inside, and the admission startled him because it was so exact. He used to laugh easily, feel pride in a well-crafted interface, look forward to weekend hikes with his wife. Now those emotions are muffled, as if heard through a thick wall. He has come to believe that there is something fundamentally wrong with him—a defect in his core wiring that made him unable to handle what happened, unable to move on. Other people survive illness and return to normal. He did not. That must mean he is weak. A weak person. The word follows him through his days, planted in the space where confidence used to be.

His marriage has strained under the weight of his avoidance. His wife does not understand why he will not go to the doctor, why he flinches from her touch, why he seems to be waiting for the next disaster. She has started to withdraw too, and the distance between them aches in a way Minh cannot articulate. He came to therapy because she asked him to, and because he is tired. Tired of the vigilance, the numbness, the certainty that he is broken. He hopes, warily, that somewhere inside him there is still a person who can feel safe. He is afraid there is not.
